input:
This pricing case examines a SaaS tier that is currently priced at $206 per unit, with a variable cost of $142 per unit and fixed costs of $475k per year. Each unit sold therefore contributes $64 towards covering the fixed costs and, ultimately, generating a profit. When the fixed costs of $475k are divided by this contribution of $64 per unit, the resulting break-even volume is 7422 units per year, which is the level of sales at which the tier exactly covers its costs and neither makes nor loses money.

Encouragingly, last year's actual volume was 7940 units, which is somewhat higher than the break-even level: the 7940 units achieved last year stand above the 7422-unit break-even level, with each unit carrying $64 of contribution. The difference between the two figures is 518 units, so the tier is currently operating above break-even, and the 518 units represent the whole of the safety margin, although it has to be said that the cushion is not especially large. A decline in volume of 518 units, for example, would bring the tier back to break-even, even before any changes in price or costs are taken into account, which highlights how sensitive the position is to relatively modest changes in demand.

It is also worth bearing in mind that all of these volume figures are based on last year's actuals, and may not necessarily be representative of future performance. More importantly, the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated, which means that the question of whether the $206 price should be changed cannot really be answered from these figures alone. A higher price would increase the contribution per unit above $64 and reduce the break-even volume below 7422 units, but what such a change would do to the current volume of 7940 units remains unknown, and could potentially offset the apparent gain.
